title: Starting a Hospice Program in Montana: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction

Starting a Hospice Program in Montana represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals with terminal illnesses while building a compliant, sustainable care business. The need for compassionate end-of-life care is profound, and Montana’s unique geography presents both challenges and significant opportunities for dedicated providers. Oversight and funding are primarily administered by the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS), Licensure Bureau, with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through Medicare and supplemental programs like the state’s Big Sky Waiver.

With moderately below demand levels in rural areas, particularly in the eastern part of the state, and reimbursement rates like $210.13 per day for Routine Home Care, Montana offers a market with significant opportunity for growth for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. The market is characterized by a concentration of services in urban centers, leaving vast regions underserved. This creates a clear path for new agencies focused on accessibility, quality, and specialized care models.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice Program in Montana, from understanding the complex regulatory landscape and licensing procedures to developing a sound business plan, hiring qualified staff, and preparing for state and federal inspections. Whether you aim to provide in-home services to a frontier community or establish a specialized inpatient facility, this framework will provide the clarity you need to succeed.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Montana’s Hospice Program Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Montana’s Hospice Program Regulations

Navigating the regulatory environment is the first and most critical step in establishing your hospice agency. Montana regulates Hospice Programs through the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS), Licensure Bureau. This state body is responsible for the initial licensing and ongoing oversight of hospice programs to ensure they meet state-specific operational and safety standards.

Beyond state licensure, any provider seeking reimbursement from Medicare must achieve certification by complying with the federal Medicare Conditions of Participation (CoPs) under 42 CFR Part 418. These federal frameworks are extensive and form the backbone of hospice operations nationwide. They dictate everything from the composition of the interdisciplinary team to the content of patient care plans and the scope of services that must be offered. Providers must also adhere to other federal rules, including HIPAA for patient privacy.

The regulatory framework in Montana, guided by the federal CoPs, emphasizes a holistic, patient-centered approach to end-of-life care, ensuring quality, compassion, and adherence to both state and federal standards. Key themes include comprehensive patient assessments, robust interdisciplinary care planning, effective pain and symptom management, and protecting patient rights. Licenses in Montana typically require renewal every 1-2 years, contingent upon successful surveys and continued compliance. Staying current with any changes from both DPHHS and CMS is non-negotiable for long-term success.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Once you understand the regulatory landscape, you can define the specific service model for your hospice. Montana supports multiple Hospice Program variants and service niches, each with different operational, staffing, and strategic requirements. While the core license is for a “Hospice Program,” your business model can be tailored to meet specific community needs.

Key service models and niches to consider include:

  • Rural and Frontier In-Home Hospice Care: This model focuses on bringing routine hospice services directly to patients in sparsely populated areas, particularly in eastern Montana where access is limited. It requires a strong logistical framework for managing travel and staff deployment.
  • Specialized Pediatric Hospice: Providing palliative and hospice care for children with life-limiting illnesses requires specialized staff training, unique care planning protocols, and close collaboration with pediatric specialists.
  • Culturally Competent Care for Native American Communities: Developing a program that respects and integrates the cultural, spiritual, and traditional values of Montana’s Native American populations can fill a critical service gap and build deep community trust.
  • In-Patient Hospice Facilities: While most hospice care is provided at home, there is a need for freestanding or hospital-based inpatient units to manage complex symptoms or provide respite care. A new facility opening in Western Montana in 2025 highlights the demand for this model.

Program size is typically measured by patient caseload. While there is no mandated capacity range, staffing ratios provide a guideline. For routine home care, a case manager might handle a caseload of 10-12 patients (based on a 1:10 ratio). The size of your agency will depend on your service area, staffing capacity, and business goals. Demand is strongest in urban centers like Missoula and Billings, but these markets also have more competition. In contrast, rural and eastern regions of Montana may offer significant entry opportunities with less competition but require a robust plan for serving a geographically dispersed population.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

With a clear service model, the next step is to establish the legal and administrative foundation of your business. Most hospice providers in Montana operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC), S-Corporation, or C-Corporation to protect personal assets from business liabilities. Consulting with a legal and financial advisor is crucial to select the best structure for your goals.

To become a licensed and operational entity, you must complete several key steps:

  • Register your business entity with the Montana Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and opening a business bank account.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including professional liability (malpractice), general liability, and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS), Licensure Bureau. This application requires detailed information about your business structure, key personnel, proposed services, and policies and procedures.

After submitting your state application, you will also need to begin the process for Medicare certification, which involves a separate application (Form CMS-855A) and a certification survey. The entire licensing and certification timeline generally ranges from 6 to 12 months, but this can be longer depending on the completeness of your application, your readiness for the initial licensure survey, and DPHHS processing times.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A detailed business plan is your roadmap to a financially viable hospice agency. It should include a thorough market analysis, operational plans, and, most importantly, a detailed financial pro forma.

Startup costs for a hospice in Montana typically range from $200,000 to $600,000. This capital covers initial licensing and consulting fees, office rent and setup, purchase of an Electronic Medical Record (EMR) system, initial payroll before revenue begins, marketing expenses, and securing necessary insurance. Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing, which often represents approximately 60-70% of total costs. This includes salaries, benefits, payroll taxes, and mileage reimbursement for your clinical team.

Your revenue will be generated primarily through the Medicare Hospice Benefit, which pays a per diem (daily) rate for each patient. Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in Montana include:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): The most common level of care, reimbursed at approximately $210.13 per day.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): For patients in crisis, this is billed hourly. Nurse add-on rates are approximately $63.44 per unit (a unit is typically 15 minutes or an hour, per payer rules).
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): For short-term care in a facility to manage acute symptoms, reimbursed at a much higher daily rate.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Short-term inpatient care to provide a break for family caregivers, reimbursed at a specific daily rate.

Successful hospice providers operating at a target utilization of 70-80% of their staffed capacity can generally achieve healthy 15-25% gross profit margins. Your business plan should project your patient census growth over the first 1-2 years and forecast your break-even point, which typically occurs between 12 and 18 months of operation.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Even if you plan to provide all care in patients’ homes, you must have a physical office that serves as your administrative hub and meets regulatory requirements. For providers considering an inpatient unit, the facility requirements are far more extensive.

For a standard hospice agency office, facility requirements include:

  • HIPAA-compliant record storage for both physical and electronic patient files.
  • An office space that is accessible to staff and, if applicable, the public, complying with ADA standards.
  • Sufficient space for the interdisciplinary team to hold regular meetings.
  • Compliance with all local zoning, fire safety, and building codes.
  • A secure area for storing medical supplies and equipment.

If you plan to open an inpatient hospice facility, you will need to meet hospital-like standards, including patient rooms designed for comfort and privacy, nursing stations, common areas for families, medication rooms, and specialized equipment. Location selection is strategic. You should choose a location that considers zoning laws, accessibility for patients’ families, proximity to key referral sources like hospitals and oncology clinics, and the availability of a qualified healthcare workforce.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

The quality of your hospice is determined by the quality of your team. Assembling a compassionate, skilled, and compliant staff is paramount. Per Medicare regulations, care must be managed by an Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) that meets regularly to coordinate care for every patient.

Required roles for your hospice team typically include:

  • Administrator/Director: Oversees all agency operations. In Montana, this role often requires a Bachelor’s degree in Nursing, Social Work, or Health Administration.
  • Medical Director: A physician who provides medical oversight, certifies patient eligibility, and consults with the IDG.
  • Registered Nurse (RN) Case Manager: Manages the patient’s clinical care, develops the plan of care, and supervises other clinical staff.
  • Social Worker (MSW preferred): Addresses the psychosocial needs of the patient and family.
  • Spiritual Counselor/Chaplain: Provides spiritual support aligned with the patient’s and family’s beliefs.
  • Bereavement Coordinator: Manages the bereavement program, providing support to families for up to 13 months after the patient’s death.
  • Hospice Aides: Provide personal care to patients under the supervision of an RN.

Training is a major focus of regulatory compliance. Montana requires 40 hours of initial training for direct care staff like hospice aides. All staff must receive orientation on hospice philosophy, policies, and procedures. Furthermore, Medicare requires ongoing training, annual competency evaluations, and discipline-specific continuing education to ensure the team remains proficient and up-to-date on best practices in end-of-life care.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your agency cannot operate without a comprehensive set of written policies and procedures. These documents are the operational playbook for your agency, ensuring consistent, compliant, and high-quality care. They will be reviewed in detail during your state licensure and Medicare certification surveys.

Montana and federal regulations require written policies covering a wide range of topics, including:

  • Patient Rights and Responsibilities
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) Operations and Care Planning
  • Plan of Care Development, Review, and Implementation
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Infection Control and Prevention
  • Emergency Preparedness Plan
  • Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI)
  • Volunteer Program Management and Training
  • Bereavement Services for Families
  • Staffing and Supervision

At the heart of hospice care is the individual care plan. This document must be developed by the IDG in collaboration with the patient and family within days of admission. It must be a dynamic document, reviewed and updated regularly to reflect the patient’s changing needs and goals. Meticulous documentation of care plans and IDG meetings is essential for both quality care and survey compliance.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike many other businesses, hospice marketing is not about direct-to-consumer advertising. Instead, it is a professional, relationship-based effort focused on educating and building trust with healthcare professionals who make referrals.

In Montana, referrals for hospice care typically come from:

  • Hospitals (Discharge Planners and Case Managers)
  • Oncologists and other specialists (Cardiologists, Pulmonologists)
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs)
  • Primary Care Physicians
  • Assisted Living Facilities
  • Home Health Agencies

Your marketing strategy should involve hiring a community liaison or healthcare marketer who can systematically visit these sources, provide education on your agency’s specific services and capabilities, and demonstrate your value proposition. Successful providers focus on demonstrating compliance, responsiveness, and excellent clinical outcomes rather than flashy advertising. Building a reputation as a reliable partner who makes the referral process easy and provides exceptional patient care is the most effective marketing tool you have.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Achieving licensure and certification is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Your hospice will be subject to ongoing oversight and periodic inspections (surveys) to ensure you continue to meet all state and federal requirements.

Oversight includes unannounced surveys from the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS), Licensure Bureau, and, for Medicare-certified agencies, a CMS-approved accrediting organization (like CHAP or ACHC) or the state survey agency acting on behalf of CMS. These inspections are rigorous and focus on direct observation of patient care, clinical record reviews, and staff interviews.

Surveyors often focus on areas where agencies commonly fall short. Common deficiencies in hospice care include:

  • Incomplete, inconsistent, or outdated Plans of Care.
  • Failure to conduct and document comprehensive patient assessments.
  • Inadequate documentation of IDG meetings and care coordination.
  • Errors in medication management and reconciliation.
  • Lack of documented supervision for hospice aides.
  • A weak or non-functional Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program.

To avoid these pitfalls, you must foster a culture of continuous quality improvement. Your QAPI program should be an active, data-driven process used to identify and correct problems. Maintaining audit-ready documentation at all times is not just a best practice—it’s essential for survival.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to open a Hospice Program in Montana?

  • The process typically takes 12 to 18 months from initial planning to receiving your first patient. This timeline includes business entity formation, developing policies, the state licensing application process, the Medicare certification process, and initial marketing to build a census.

What licenses are required to operate a hospice in Montana?

  • You need a Hospice Program license from the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS), Licensure Bureau. To receive payment from Medicare, which is the primary payer for hospice, you must also achieve Medicare certification by meeting the Conditions of Participation found in 42 CFR Part 418.

What reimbursement is available for hospice services in Montana?

  • Reimbursement primarily comes from the Medicare Hospice Benefit, which pays a per diem rate based on the level of care provided. In Montana, the Routine Home Care rate is approximately $210.13 per day. Other levels of care, like Continuous Home Care and General Inpatient Care, have different reimbursement structures. Private insurance may also cover hospice, and some related services may be supported by programs like Montana’s Big Sky Waiver.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice Program in Montana is a challenging yet incredibly rewarding venture. It requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. The market holds clear opportunities, especially for providers willing to serve rural and frontier communities or offer specialized programs.

Providers who invest in a strong foundation of compliance, hire and train a compassionate and skilled team, and build trusting relationships with referral sources are positioned for long-term success and sustainability. By focusing on quality and patient-centered care, you can build a business that not only thrives financially but also makes a profound difference in the lives of Montanans at the end of life.
